title: Profiling & Debugging Kernels
blurb: Tests which tool answers which question: nvidia-smi, torch.profiler, Nsight Systems, Nsight Compute and compute-sanitizer, why a launch can "succeed" while writing out of bounds, the ncu permissions error, and what the measurements overturned.

refLinks.label: §46.2.1 nvidia-smi: The Free Glance Before Any of the Above
§46.2.3 Nsight Systems: Finding the Bottleneck, Not Guessing It
§46.2.4 Nsight Compute: Going Deeper on One Kernel

questions.prompt: Which tool answers "which kernel is the bottleneck?" across a whole program?
options: Nsight Compute (ncu) profiler
cudaGetLastError()
compute-sanitizer
Nsight Systems (nsys)
questions.explanation: nsys records a timeline and summarises time per kernel. ncu explains one kernel in depth. compute-sanitizer checks correctness. cudaGetLastError only reports launch failures.

options: ncu costs far more per kernel, so aim it first.
nsys needs elevated permissions, which ncu then reuses.
ncu only works on kernels that nsys has never profiled.
ncu can't run until nsys has created a profile file for it to read.
questions.explanation: Deep-diving with ncu on a kernel that turns out not to matter wastes its overhead. nsys finds the bottleneck cheaply first.

questions.prompt: Output is wrong and compute-sanitizer reports 0 errors. What does that rule out, and what is left?
options: All bugs are ruled out, so the expected output must be wrong.
Nothing. compute-sanitizer only works on fast kernels.
Performance bugs are ruled out, so use ncu next.
Memory bugs are out. Check the maths next.
questions.explanation: compute-sanitizer catches memory, race and sync classes of bug. A pure logic error that never touches invalid memory passes it cleanly.

questions.prompt: A program seems hung. What does the chapter suggest checking first?
options: compute-sanitizer, since hangs are always memory bugs
ncu, to read the warp stall reasons of whatever kernel is running
torch.profiler, wrapped around the whole program
nvidia-smi, to see whether the GPU is doing anything at all
questions.explanation: It costs nothing and needs no code change. An idle GPU points upstream, to the CPU side. A GPU at 100% points to a running kernel worth profiling.

refLinks.label: §46.2.1 nvidia-smi: The Free Glance Before Any of the Above

questions.prompt: nvidia-smi reads 0% once. Why isn't that proof the GPU is unused?
options: nvidia-smi can't see kernels launched from Python.
It's one instant, and a CPU-side stall reads 0% too.
0% means the GPU is at full speed, since it reports idle time.
nvidia-smi only reports memory, never utilisation.
questions.explanation: Poll repeatedly across the run. A tight loop of fast kernels can be idle between launches, and a program blocked on a lock or I/O reads 0% for a different reason.

questions.prompt: Why is torch.profiler the natural first tool for a PyTorch pipeline?
options: It checks every memory access for out-of-bounds errors.
It shows hardware counters such as warp stalls for each kernel.
It gives an op-level breakdown from inside Python.
It is the only tool that sees cuBLAS kernels at all.
questions.explanation: Wrap the code in profile(...) and sort key_averages by CUDA time. Hardware counters are ncu's job, and memory checking is compute-sanitizer's.

questions.prompt: In nsys's per-kernel summary, why does the Instances column matter?
options: It shows how many SMs the kernel used on each launch.
It counts the errors that kernel raised across all of its launches.
It counts threads per block, which sets occupancy.
A kernel called many times can dominate even if each call is fast.
questions.explanation: Total time is per-call time times call count. Avg (ns) separates a per-call cost from one driven by how often the kernel runs.

questions.prompt: which_tool in Listing 46.3 gets the symptom 'inconsistent_across_runs'. What does it return, and why that order?
options: ncu, to read the hardware counters of the slow kernel
nvidia-smi, to see if the GPU is busy
compute-sanitizer, to rule out memory bugs first
nsys, to see which kernel takes the most time
questions.explanation: Wrong, flaky or crashing output goes to compute-sanitizer first. Ruling out a memory bug is often faster than reviewing the algorithm by hand.

questions.prompt: Running ncu as a normal user gives ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM. What is going on?
options: nsys is already running and holds the counters.
ncu doesn't support the RTX 5090.
The driver limits counters to admins by default.
The kernel has a bug that blocks profiling.
questions.explanation: It's the default security posture on most Linux installs, not a broken setup. Fix it with sudo, or a driver setting and a reboot. nsys and compute-sanitizer work without it.

refLinks.label: §46.2.4 Nsight Compute: Going Deeper on One Kernel

questions.prompt: On a shared cluster with no root access, which tools remain usable? Select all that apply.
options: compute-sanitizer
ncu with full hardware counters
nsys
nvidia-smi
questions.explanation: The chapter says nsys and compute-sanitizer are unaffected by the counter restriction. nvidia-smi ships with the driver. Full ncu counters need elevated permissions.

questions.prompt: Why did the off-by-one kernel report "cudaGetLastError: no error"?
options: Out-of-bounds writes are allowed on modern GPUs.
The bug writes inside the buffer, so there is nothing at all to report.
Error checking is off unless the code is compiled with -G.
It only checks whether the launch was rejected, not each memory access.
questions.explanation: cudaGetLastError catches bad grid sizes and resource limits. An out-of-bounds access can corrupt other data silently, which is why a separate correctness tool exists.

questions.prompt: Why compile with nvcc -lineinfo before running compute-sanitizer?
options: It adds bounds checks to every array access.
So reports name a file and line, at no runtime cost.
Without it, compute-sanitizer can't detect any errors.
It turns off optimisation, which hides memory bugs.
questions.explanation: Errors are still detected without it, but only as offsets. The procedure's common mistake is debugging from raw addresses alone.

questions.prompt: The buggy kernel launched 1,024 threads over n = 1,000 elements with the check i <= n. Which global index is the first to go out of bounds?
questions.explanation: Valid indices are 0 to 999. i <= n lets i = 1000 through. The sanitizer named thread 232 in block 3: 3 × 256 + 232 = 1000.

questions.prompt: The sanitizer named thread 232 in block 3 for an index of 1000. What block size does that imply?
questions.explanation: blockIdx × blockDim + threadIdx = 1000, so 3 × blockDim + 232 = 1000 and blockDim = 768 / 3 = 256.

questions.prompt: Which kernel dominated the nsys profile of vecAdd, sigmoid and tree reduction?
options: The sigmoid kernel, because expf is expensive
All three took equal time
The tree reduction, at 56.3%
vecAdd, because it moves the most data
questions.explanation: The guess that expf would dominate was wrong. The reduction's barriers and final atomic cost more. That is the reason to profile instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: torch.profiler showed the matmul at 96.8% of GPU time, as anyone would guess. What does the chapter take from that?
options: torch.profiler is less accurate than nsys, so the result can't be trusted.
Sometimes intuition is right. Profiling says when.
Profiling PyTorch is pointless, since the matmul always dominates.
The sigmoid and sum must have been mis-measured.
questions.explanation: Set beside the nsys surprise, the point is that you don't know in advance which way it will go. Measure either way.

questions.prompt: A training job gives slightly different losses on reruns with the same seed, and sometimes NaN. A teammate wants to rewrite the custom kernel's maths. What should come first?
options: Run nsys to see which kernel takes the most time.
Run ncu to find the kernel's warp stall reasons.
Run it under compute-sanitizer to rule out a memory or race bug.
Rewrite the maths, since NaNs always mean an error in the formula.
questions.explanation: Inconsistent and unpredictable output is exactly the symptom Procedure 46.3 sends to compute-sanitizer. Performance tools won't find a correctness bug.

bookExercises.prompt: State which of the three tools, `nsys`, `ncu`, `compute-sanitizer`, answers each question: (a) "which of my five kernels is slowest overall?"; (b) "is this kernel reading past the end of an allocation?"; (c) "why is this one kernel only achieving 40% memory throughput?"
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) `nsys`: a system-wide timeline profiler that reports which of several kernels dominates overall time. (b) `compute-sanitizer`: a runtime correctness checker for out-of-bounds and other memory-safety bugs. (c) `ncu`: a deep per-kernel hardware-counter profiler that explains why one specific kernel is slow (memory throughput, occupancy, stalls).

bookExercises.prompt: Explain why `cudaGetLastError()` reported "no error" for the buggy kernel in this chapter's Worked Example, even though the kernel performed an invalid memory access.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `cudaGetLastError()` only reports launch and execution-configuration errors, not out-of-bounds memory accesses within a kernel. An invalid read/write to global memory is not treated by the CUDA runtime as an "error" the way a malformed launch would be. It simply reads or corrupts whatever memory happens to be at that address, silently, unless a dedicated correctness tool is used to catch it.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 46.6, compute what percentage of total pipeline time `sumTreeReduction` would need to drop to if it were optimized down to `vecAdd`'s average per-launch time, assuming `vecAdd` and `sigmoidKernel`'s times stay fixed.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Total pipeline time per iteration ≈ 21,811 + 8,582 + 8,429 = 38,822 ns. If `sumTreeReduction` dropped to `vecAdd`'s average (8,582 ns), new total ≈ 8,582 + 8,582 + 8,429 = 25,593 ns. `sumTreeReduction`'s new share of the reduced total ≈ 8,582 / 25,593 ≈ 33.5%, down from 56.2%.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague's kernel is compiled without `-lineinfo` and `compute-sanitizer` reports an address instead of a file:line. Write the corrected `nvcc` command that would fix this, referencing Procedure 46.2.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `nvcc -arch=sm_XX -lineinfo --ptxas-options=-v yourfile.cu -o yourfile`. Adding `-lineinfo` embeds source file/line debug information so `compute-sanitizer` can report a file:line instead of a bare address.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 46.3 as a model, extend `which_tool` with a new symptom string, `'high_kernel_launch_count'`, and decide which of the three tools (or a fourth answer) is the right response, justifying the choice.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Extending `which_tool` with `'high_kernel_launch_count'`: this symptom points toward CUDA API call overhead rather than a single kernel's internal performance, so the right response is `nsys stats --report cuda_api_sum`, not `ncu`. `ncu` profiles inside one kernel's execution, while excessive launch count is an orchestration/overhead problem `nsys`'s API summary report is built to diagnose.

bookExercises.prompt: A teammate wants to skip `nsys` and go straight to `ncu --set full` on every kernel in a ten-kernel pipeline "to be thorough." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two-sentence case against this approach.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `ncu --set full` collects a large, slow set of hardware counters per kernel; running it on all ten kernels "to be thorough" multiplies a heavy per-kernel cost by ten before knowing which kernels even matter. `nsys` first identifies the one or two kernels that actually dominate total time, so `ncu --set full` can then be spent only where it will change a decision. Reversing the order wastes far more profiling time for the same eventual insight.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's `ncu` permission error is described as "not a sign of a broken setup." Propose a one-sentence addition to a team's onboarding documentation that would prevent a new engineer from wasting an afternoon debugging their CUDA install because of this error.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Suggested addition: "If `ncu` reports `ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`, this is a standard OS-level permissions restriction, not a broken CUDA install. Either run `ncu` with `sudo` or ask your admin to set `NVreg_RestrictProfilingToAdminUsers=0`. `nsys` and `compute-sanitizer` are unaffected and can be used in the meantime."

bookExercises.prompt: Skim the NVIDIA Nsight Compute documentation's metric reference. Pick one hardware counter not named in this chapter (occupancy, memory throughput, and warp stall reasons were all mentioned) and explain in one or two sentences what question it would help answer.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, depends on which counter is chosen (e.g. warp stall reasons beyond the ones named, L2 cache hit rate, or achieved occupancy vs. theoretical occupancy). The exercise is to connect a specific, named Nsight Compute metric to a specific diagnostic question it answers that this chapter's three named categories (occupancy, memory throughput, stall reasons) don't directly cover.

bookExercises.prompt: A program that should take a few seconds appears to hang indefinitely, and `nvidia-smi` reads 0% GPU utilisation the entire time. Using this chapter's Procedure 46.5, name two structurally different root causes consistent with that single reading, and state what a next step to distinguish them would be.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Two structurally different root causes consistent with 0% GPU utilisation the whole time: (1) the program is stuck on the CPU side entirely, before it ever reaches a kernel launch (blocked on a lock, waiting on I/O, stuck in a host-side loop), so the GPU is correctly idle because it has genuinely been given no work yet; (2) the program launched its work and crashed or deadlocked in a way that never actually issued the kernel to the device (a host-side exception swallowed silently, a CUDA API call that failed before any kernel launch). `nvidia-smi` alone cannot distinguish these; the next step is attaching a CPU-side debugger or profiler (or simply checking whether the host process is still consuming CPU time) to see whether execution is progressing on the host at all.
